summary: Describes a simple username and password authentication method for the SOCKS version 5 setup. It fits into the authentication subnegotiation framework that SOCKS5 defines.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the doorman lets you through, you show a name and a secret word. This note defines how that name-and-password check is done.

subtitle: The simple username and password login step used by SOCKS version 5.

tldr.problem: SOCKS version 5 provides a framework for authentication subnegotiation but needs concrete methods that fit it.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a version byte, the username and the password, each with a length, and the server replies with a version and a status byte where zero means success.
tldr.outcome: The password travels in cleartext, so the RFC does not recommend it where sniffing is possible and practical.

today: RFC 1929 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where This Fits in SOCKS V5
sections.content:
The SOCKS Version 5 specification defines a framework that allows arbitrary authentication protocols during connection setup. This document describes one of them, Username/Password Authentication, as it fits into the SOCKS V5 authentication subnegotiation.

Once the SOCKS V5 server has started and the client has selected this method, the subnegotiation begins. The packet diagrams show field lengths in octets, and X'hh' marks a specific octet value.
sections.plainLanguage: SOCKS lets you choose how to prove who you are. This is one way: a name and a password.

sections.title: Request and Response
sections.content:
The client sends a request with five fields: VER (1 octet, X'01'), ULEN (1 octet, length of the username), UNAME (1 to 255 octets, the username as known to the source operating system), PLEN (1 octet) and PASSWD (1 to 255 octets).

The server checks the credentials and replies with VER and a one-octet STATUS. A STATUS of X'00' means success. Any other value is a failure, and the server MUST close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends its name and password, each with a note of how long it is. The server answers with a yes or no code, and hangs up on a no.

sections.title: Cleartext Passwords
sections.content: The request carries the password in cleartext. For that reason the RFC says the subnegotiation is not recommended for environments where sniffing is possible and practical.
sections.plainLanguage: The password is sent as plain writing, so anyone listening on the wire could read it.

messages.label: VER, STATUS
messages.note: X'00' means success; anything else and the server MUST close.
